source.title: MoReBench: Evaluating Procedural and Pluralistic Moral Reasoning in Language Models, More than Outcomes
source.authors: Yu Ying Chiu; Michael S. Lee; Rachel Calcott; B. Handoko; P. de Font-Reaulx; Raphaël Millière; Paula Rodriguez; Chen Bo Calvin Zhang; Ziwen Han; Udari Madhushani Sehwag; Yash Maurya; Christina Q. Knight; Harry R. Lloyd; Florence Bacus; C. record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some tables are flattened in the text extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares moral-reasoning benchmark scores across model sizes and reports that the expected larger-model advantage does not consistently hold. This challenges the predictability-with-scale part of V6, but it does not measure pretraining loss or test the original loss-scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports rubric-judge F1 scores, moral-reasoning dimensions, theory-specific results, and correlations with other benchmarks. Those are not rows for the scale comparison unless they directly measure predictability with scale; benchmark-to-benchmark correlations are recorded under fits_no_version. The model-family results below are the aggregate trends explicitly stated in the text; detailed per-checkpoint scores also appear in Tables 6 and 7.
record.test_reason: Section 4.1 and Appendix G.3 ask whether larger models in a family score higher on MoReBench. The authors argue scaling expectations fail for moral reasoning. This bears on V6, whether downstream performance improves with scale. It is a weak test. Scale is the product tier within a family, parameter counts are unstated for closed models, tiers differ in version and post-training, and no loss or functional form is fitted.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say scaling laws and STEM benchmarks fail to predict moral-reasoning performance. They attribute the Regular-score non-monotonicity to smaller models writing longer traces, and cite the partial reversal under length correction as support. Note: their G.3 text claims the smallest Claude and Qwen models are best on final responses, but Table 7 shows the larger models scoring higher.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates moral-reasoning benchmark scores across existing model variants; it does not fit pretraining-loss scaling laws or reproduce either original study's training sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The model-size pattern differs between MoReBench-Regular and length-corrected MoReBench-Hard. The paper also reports different size trends across model families.

fits_no_version.finding: MoReBench scores correlate weakly or negligibly with Chatbot Arena, HLE, AIME 25 and LiveCodeBench across 14 models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: General capability and STEM benchmarks do not predict moral-reasoning benchmark scores.

record.problems: The paper reports benchmark scores for existing model variants rather than a controlled training sweep; model parameter counts are not stated for most variants. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss. The text gives qualitative family-level size trends, while detailed checkpoint scores are presented in tables.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed per-checkpoint score results in Tables 6 and 7 were not separately extracted; the rows record the family-level size trends explicitly described in Sections 4.1 and G.3. No other benchmark results were included unless they directly addressed scale predictability.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Performance as a function of pretraining loss; any fitted or predictive functional form; scale beyond 2–3 product tiers of unknown size.

missing.what: Final-response MoReBench-Hard size trends. GPT-5: high 18.2 > mini 15.7 > nano 12.0. Claude: Sonnet 30.6 > Opus 28.8. Gemini: Lite 13.7 > Pro 12.2 > Flash 11.7. GPT-oss: 20b 14.1 > 120b 11.3. Qwen: 235B 12.9 ≈ 30B 12.6.
Per-model scores for every within-family comparison; the rows give only qualitative text.
MoReBench-Theory within-family size comparisons. For example, thinking-trace overall scores: GPT-oss 20b 70.3 > 120b 68.2; Qwen 30B 73.7 ≈ 235B 73.6.

record.verdict_notes: 'Scale' here is product tier, not measured parameters; closed-model sizes are undisclosed, and Claude compares Opus 4.1 with Sonnet 4. No uncertainty is given for score differences, several of which are under 1 point. The Hard metric divides by length, so it is confounded with verbosity. This is a weak, indirect test of V6 only.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute.
Whether power laws fitted on small pretraining runs predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations at fixed compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.

The study tests moral-reasoning benchmark performance across model variants, not downstream task performance as a function of pretraining loss. It does not establish a general relationship across downstream tasks.
Fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, and their dependence on fitting or training setup.

source_check.notes:
The supplied text is arXiv v2 dated June 2026. G.3 prose contradicts Table 7 for Claude and Qwen3 final responses.
Closed-model size comparisons use product tiers; the study does not control training scale, fit scaling laws, or report uncertainty for these ranking differences. Hard measures score per response length, and closed-model thinking traces can be summaries.

Section 3.2 defines Hard as the Regular score multiplied by 1000 divided by average response length in characters.
